## Introduction

### Overview

In these exercises, you'll keep exploring the RNA-seq gene count table from this week's lectures,
practicing the R material from weeks 12 and 13
in a few different ways:

- In Exercise 1, you'll **predict** the output of code before running it.
- In Exercise 2, you'll **find and fix** the mistakes in some code,
  and see which of them Claude can find.
- In Exercise 3, you'll **wrangle data** to answer a biological question,
  and learn a new function to search text.
- In Exercise 4, you'll **recreate** a plot from just an image.
- In Exercise 5, you'll make and customize a **violin plot**.
- In Exercise 6, you'll use **Claude** to polish a plot.

::: callout-tip
#### Lecture page exercises
As usual, make sure to do any of the exercises on this week's lecture pages
that we didn't do in class.
Also, if you struggled with any of the exercises we did do in class,
go over those again.
:::

### Setting up

1. Open Positron and connect to OSC
   [like in week 12](/week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#setup-starting-positron-and-connecting-to-osc),
   and open the `week13` folder that you created in this week's lectures.

2. Create a new Quarto document `week13/w13_exercises.qmd`,
   with a YAML header with a title, your name, and the date.

3. Add the following code chunk to the top of your document,
   which loads the tidyverse, reads the two tables from the lectures
   plus a gene annotation table (see [below](#the-gene-annotation-table)),
   and makes a long version of the count table that includes the metadata:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

# Read the count table, metadata, and gene annotation table
counts <- read_tsv(
  "/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv"
) |>
  select(!gene_name)
meta <- read_tsv("../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv") |>
  # Make `time` a factor, so 24 hpi comes before 10 dpi in plots
  mutate(time = factor(time, levels = c("24hpi", "10dpi")))
genes <- read_tsv("/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/genes.tsv")

# Make a long-format count table, with the metadata added
counts_long <- counts |>
  pivot_longer(cols = !gene_id, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "count") |>
  left_join(meta, by = "sample_id")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

counts <- read_tsv(
  "../assets/week13/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv"
) |>
  select(!gene_name)
meta <- read_tsv("../assets/week13/metadata.tsv") |>
  mutate(time = factor(time, levels = c("24hpi", "10dpi")))
genes <- read_tsv("../assets/week13/genes.tsv")

counts_long <- counts |>
  pivot_longer(cols = !gene_id, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "count") |>
  left_join(meta, by = "sample_id")
```

### The gene annotation table

The count table only has gene IDs, which don't tell you what the genes are.
That information is in the genome annotation (GTF) file.
To make things easier, we've extracted a table from this file,
which you read into `genes` above.
It has one row per gene, and these columns:

- `gene_id`: Gene ID, as in the count table
- `chromosome`: Chromosome (`chr1`--`chr3` and `MT` for the mitochondrial genome),
  or `NA` for genes on smaller pieces of the genome assembly that have not been placed on a chromosome
- `biotype`: Type of gene, such as `protein_coding` or `lncRNA`
- `description`: Description of the gene product
- `transcript_length`: Length (bp) of the gene's longest transcript

```{r}
genes
```

You'll use this table in Exercises 3 and 5.

::: callout-tip
#### General tips for the exercises

- Install any packages that you haven't installed yet in the console,
  _not_ in your Quarto document.
  Apart from installing packages, run all your code in code chunks.
- Add a header for each exercise to your document,
  so it's easy to navigate the rendered document using the table of contents.
- Render your document every now and then, to catch problems early.
:::

## Exercise 1: Predict the output

For each question, first decide on your answer,
and then run the code to check whether you were right.

1. Which samples will this code keep?

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   meta |>
     filter(time == "24hpi", treatment != "control")
   ```

   a) Only the control samples at 24 hpi
   b) Only the _cathemerium_ and _relictum_ samples at 24 hpi
   c) The _cathemerium_ and _relictum_ samples at both time points
   d) All samples at 24 hpi, plus the _cathemerium_ and _relictum_ samples at 10 dpi

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   **b)** is correct:

   ```{r}
   meta |>
     filter(time == "24hpi", treatment != "control")
   ```

   Because the two conditions are separated by a comma,
   a row has to meet _both_ of them.
   Answer **d)** contains the rows that meet _either_ condition,
   which is what you'd get with `|` instead of a comma.

   </details>

2. What will this code return?

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   mean(counts$S63 > 0)
   ```

   a) The mean count of sample `S63`
   b) A `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each gene
   c) The proportion of genes with at least one read in sample `S63`
   d) An error, because you can't compute the mean of logicals

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   **c)** is correct:

   ```{r}
   mean(counts$S63 > 0)
   ```

   The comparison returns a `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each gene,
   and because `TRUE` counts as 1 and `FALSE` as 0,
   the mean of these logicals is the proportion of `TRUE`s:
   `r round(100 * mean(counts$S63 > 0))`% of genes were detected in sample `S63`.
   This is the same as `sum(counts$S63 > 0) / nrow(counts)`,
   but shorter.

   </details>

3. What will each row of this code's output represent?

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   counts_long |>
     summarize(total = sum(count), .by = c(treatment, time))
   ```

   a) One time point
   b) One treatment
   c) One combination of treatment and time point
   d) One sample

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   **c)** is correct:

   ```{r}
   counts_long |>
     summarize(total = sum(count), .by = c(treatment, time))
   ```

   When you group by two columns,
   you get one row for each _combination_ of their values.

   </details>

4. Which of these lines of code return the same result?

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   round(mean(counts$S63), 1)
   round(digits = 1, x = mean(counts$S63))
   round(1, mean(counts$S63))
   ```

   a) All three
   b) Only the first two
   c) Only the first and the third
   d) None

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   **b)** is correct:

   ```{r}
   round(mean(counts$S63), 1)
   round(digits = 1, x = mean(counts$S63))
   round(1, mean(counts$S63))
   ```

   - In the first line, the arguments are not named,
     so R matches them by position: first `x`, then `digits`.
   - In the second line, the arguments are named, so their order doesn't matter.
   - In the third line, the arguments are not named but in the "wrong" order,
     so R rounds the number 1 to about 1,289 digits, which is still 1.
     Note that R doesn't give an error or warning here!

   </details>

5. Which plot will this code produce?
   (`geom_smooth()` adds a trend line, here a straight one from a linear model.)

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   counts_long |>
     summarize(
       lib_size_M = sum(count) / 1e6,
       n_detected = sum(count > 0),
       .by = c(sample_id, treatment)
     ) |>
     ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected)) +
     geom_point() +
     geom_smooth(aes(color = treatment), method = "lm")
   ```

   a) Points and trend lines are both colored by treatment
   b) Black points, and a separate colored trend line for each treatment
   c) Black points, and a single blue trend line

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   **b)** is correct:

   ```{r}
   #| message: false
   counts_long |>
     summarize(
       lib_size_M = sum(count) / 1e6,
       n_detected = sum(count > 0),
       .by = c(sample_id, treatment)
     ) |>
     ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected)) +
     geom_point() +
     geom_smooth(aes(color = treatment), method = "lm")
   ```

   `color = treatment` is a local mapping in `geom_smooth()`,
   so only the trend lines are colored by treatment,
   and `geom_point()` uses the default color (black).

   </details>

## Exercise 2: Find the bugs

The code below is supposed to make a plot of the library sizes of the control samples,
with the time points along the x-axis,
a box plot for each time point with a different fill color,
and the individual samples shown as points on top of the boxes.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
control_libs <- counts_long |>
  filter(treatment = "Control") |>
  summarize(lib_size_M = sum(count) / 1e6, .by = sample_id, time)

control_libs |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = lib_size_M, fill = "time")) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

1. The code contains **five mistakes** (but only two of them cause an error).
   Find and fix all of them, one by one.
   For each mistake, note whether it caused an error, and if not,
   how you noticed it.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   control_libs <- counts_long |>
     filter(treatment == "control") |>
     summarize(lib_size_M = sum(count) / 1e6, .by = c(sample_id, time))

   control_libs |>
     ggplot(aes(x = time, y = lib_size_M, fill = time)) +
     geom_boxplot() +
     geom_point(size = 3)
   ```

   The two mistakes that cause errors are:

   - `filter(treatment = "Control")` should use `==` to test for equality.
     The error message even suggests the fix.
   - `.by = sample_id, time` should be `.by = c(sample_id, time)`.
     Without `c()`, `time` is no longer part of the `.by` argument,
     and `summarize()` tries to make a column with all of the values of `time`.
     The error message (`time must be size 1`) is harder to understand,
     but it does mention `time`.

   You probably saw the second error only after you fixed the capital "C" in `"Control"`.
   That's because the three mistakes below don't cause errors:

   - `"Control"` should be `"control"`.
     R is case-sensitive, so no rows match, and `filter()` returns an empty data frame.
     You might have noticed this from the empty plot,
     or by looking at `control_libs`.
   - `fill = "time"` should not have quotes.
     With quotes, `"time"` is treated as a single fixed value,
     so both boxes get the same color, and the legend has a single entry: "time".
   - `geom_point()` should come after `geom_boxplot()`.
     Layers are drawn in the order you add them,
     so the filled boxes were drawn over the points, hiding most of them.

   </details>

2. Start a new conversation in Claude, paste the original code with the mistakes,
   and ask Claude to find the mistakes,
   _without_ telling it what the plot should look like.
   Which of the five mistakes did it find?
   Then, also give Claude the description of the intended plot above the code.
   Which mistakes could Claude only find with this description,
   or by looking at your data?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Claude's answers will differ,
   but it can find the two mistakes that cause errors from the code alone.
   It may also flag `fill = "time"`, because quoting a column name inside `aes()`
   is a common mistake.

   The other two mistakes depend on what you want, and on your data:

   - Whether `geom_point()` should come after `geom_boxplot()`
     depends on whether you want the points to be visible on top of the boxes,
     which is in the description.
   - Whether `"Control"` is wrong depends on how the treatments are spelled in your data.
     Claude can only know this if it looks at the data,
     for example by reading the metadata file,
     or by running code.

   So, the more context you give Claude, the more it can check.

   </details>

## Exercise 3: Data wrangling to explore vitellogenin genes

In this exercise, you'll find out which genes are most highly expressed,
and then see how the expression of one group of these genes differs between the time points.

1. Compute the mean count of each gene across all samples,
   and sort the genes from highest to lowest mean count.
   Can you tell from the output what the top genes are?

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>

   Use `summarize()` with the `.by` argument,
   and `arrange()` with `desc()`.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   counts_long |>
     summarize(mean_count = mean(count), .by = gene_id) |>
     arrange(desc(mean_count))
   ```

   Mostly not:
   IDs like `LOC120426760` don't tell you what the genes are.
   Only a few genes have IDs that are also gene names,
   like the mitochondrial gene `COX1`, a bit further down the list.

   </details>

2. Add the gene information from `genes` to the output of the previous step.
   To see the full gene descriptions and more than 10 rows,
   add `View()` to the end of your pipeline to open the result in the Data Explorer.
   Do you see any recurring patterns among the names of the genes at the top?
   And why do some rows have `NA`s?

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for some hints_</summary>

   - Use `left_join()` to add the gene information by combining the two data frames.
   - For the `NA`s, compare the `chromosome` column of those rows.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   counts_long |>
     summarize(mean_count = mean(count), .by = gene_id) |>
     left_join(genes, by = "gene_id") |>
     arrange(desc(mean_count))
   ```

   Several of the most highly expressed genes are **vitellogenins**,
   including the top gene.

   There are two kinds of rows with `NA`s:

   - "Unassigned genes" like `unassigned_gene_22` have `NA`s in all of the added columns.
     These genes are in the count table but not in the annotation table.
     `left_join()` keeps all rows of the first data frame,
     and fills in `NA` when there is no match in the second one.
   - Mitochondrial genes like `COX1` (chromosome `MT`) only have an `NA` description.
     They _are_ in the annotation table,
     but don't have a description there,
     probably because their gene IDs are already gene names.

   </details>

3. Vitellogenins are yolk proteins that female mosquitoes produce after a blood meal,
   to provision their eggs
   (all mosquitoes in this experiment took a blood meal at the start).
   Find all genes whose `description` in the `genes` table contains "vitellogenin".
   (This requires a new function: check the hint below.)

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>

   To do this, you need a new function, `str_detect()`, from the tidyverse's _stringr_ package.
   It checks whether each element of a character vector contains a pattern:

   ```{r}
   # Create a small mock vector of gene names
   # (In your exercise, you'll use the `description` column of the `genes` table instead.)
   gene_names <- c("vitellogenin-1", "cathepsin B-like")

   # Check which of these names contain "vitellogenin"
   str_detect(gene_names, pattern = "vitellogenin")
   ```

   Because the function returns a logical, you can use it inside `filter()`
   to keep only the rows that contain the pattern.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   genes |>
     filter(str_detect(description, pattern = "vitellogenin"))
   ```

   </details>

4. Not all the genes that contain "vitellogenin" in their description are vitellogenins:
   one of the 9 genes you found is a "putative vitellogenin *receptor*".
   Remove the receptor from the output of the previous step,
   and save the result in a data frame `vg_genes`.
   You should be left with 8 genes.

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>

   You can add a second condition to `filter()`, and `!` negates a logical.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   vg_genes <- genes |>
     filter(
       str_detect(description, pattern = "vitellogenin"),
       !str_detect(description, pattern = "receptor")
     )

   vg_genes
   ```

   </details>

5. Keep only the rows of `counts_long` for the vitellogenin genes.
   You should get 176 rows: 8 genes for each of the 22 samples.

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for some hints_</summary>

   - You can use `%in%` to keep rows that match any of several values
     (see the [`%in%` box in w13a](w13a_data-wrangling.qmd#filter-to-pick-rows-observations)).

   - To get your vector of gene IDs to keep,
     use the `$` operator to extract the `gene_id` column from `vg_genes`.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   counts_long |>
     filter(gene_id %in% vg_genes$gene_id)
   ```

   `vg_genes$gene_id` is a vector with the 8 gene IDs,
   so this does the same as typing all 8 IDs inside `c()`.

   </details>

6. Extend your code from the previous step to compute the total count of all
   vitellogenin genes for each sample, in millions.
   Keep the `treatment` and `time` columns in the output,
   and save the result as `vg_per_sample`.

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>

   `summarize()` only keeps the `.by` columns and the columns you compute.
   Because each sample has a single treatment and time point,
   you can add those columns to `.by` without changing the groups,
   like you did with `time` in Exercise 2.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   vg_per_sample <- counts_long |>
     filter(gene_id %in% vg_genes$gene_id) |>
     summarize(
       vg_count_M = sum(count) / 1e6,
       .by = c(sample_id, treatment, time)
     )

   vg_per_sample
   ```

   </details>

7. Vitellogenin counts could also differ between samples
   simply because some samples have larger libraries than others.
   Compute the _percentage_ of each sample's reads that are from vitellogenin genes,
   and save the result as `vg_pct`.
   Then, sort the samples by this percentage:
   what do you notice about the time points?

   Start by computing the library sizes like in the lecture:

   ```{r}
   lib_sizes <- counts_long |>
     summarize(lib_size_M = sum(count) / 1e6, .by = sample_id)
   ```

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>

   Join `lib_sizes` with `vg_per_sample`,
   and then compute the percentage with `mutate()`.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   vg_pct <- vg_per_sample |>
     left_join(lib_sizes, by = "sample_id") |>
     mutate(vg_pct = 100 * vg_count_M / lib_size_M)

   vg_pct |>
     arrange(vg_pct)
   ```

   All 10 dpi samples come first:
   at 10 dpi, less than 0.05% of the reads in a sample are from vitellogenin genes,
   while at 24 hpi, 7--17% of reads are from just these 8 genes.

   </details>

8. How would you explain the difference between the time points?
   And based on these numbers, would you conclude that infection with _P. relictum_
   lowers vitellogenin expression at 24 hpi?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Vitellogenins are produced in large amounts in the first days after a blood meal,
   when the mosquito provisions its eggs.
   At 24 hpi, the mosquitoes are in the middle of this,
   while 10 days later, it is long over.

   The _relictum_ samples do have the lowest vitellogenin percentages at 24 hpi:

   ```{r}
   vg_pct |>
     filter(time == "24hpi") |>
     summarize(mean_pct = mean(vg_pct), .by = treatment)
   ```

   But with only 3 or 4 samples per group and no statistical test,
   you can't draw a conclusion from this yet:
   that's what the differential expression analysis in week 15 is for.

   </details>

## Exercise 4: Recreate this plot

Using your `vg_pct` data frame from Exercise 3,
recreate the plot below as closely as you can.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4

vg_pct |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = vg_pct, fill = time)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Vitellogenin expression is much higher at 24 hpi",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Reads from vitellogenin genes (%)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

<details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for hints_</summary>

- The fill color of the boxes shows the time point.
- To remove an axis label, set it to `NULL` in `labs()`.
- The theme is `theme_bw()`, with the minor grid lines removed.

</details>

<details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

```{r, eval=FALSE}
vg_pct |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = vg_pct, fill = time)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Vitellogenin expression is much higher at 24 hpi",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Reads from vitellogenin genes (%)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

</details>

## Exercise 5: Violin plots

Is there a difference in expression levels between protein-coding genes and
lncRNA (long non-coding RNA) genes?
A **violin plot**, made with `geom_violin()`, is similar to a box plot,
but shows the full distribution of the data.

1. Like in Exercise 3, compute the mean count of each gene across all samples
   and add the gene information from `genes`.
   Then, keep only protein-coding and lncRNA genes with a mean count above 0.
   Save the result as `gene_means`.

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for some hints_</summary>

   - Start from your code for step 2 of Exercise 3, without the `arrange()` line.
   - In `filter()`, use `%in%` to keep both biotypes,
     and separate the two conditions with a comma.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   gene_means <- counts_long |>
     summarize(mean_count = mean(count), .by = gene_id) |>
     left_join(genes, by = "gene_id") |>
     filter(biotype %in% c("protein_coding", "lncRNA"), mean_count > 0)
   ```

   </details>

2. Make a violin plot with `biotype` on the x-axis and `mean_count` on the y-axis.
   You'll see that the violins are squashed against the x-axis. Why is that?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   gene_means |>
     ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) +
     geom_violin()
   ```

   A few genes have extremely high counts, so most genes are squashed near 0.
   This is typical for gene counts, which is why they are usually plotted on a log scale.

   </details>

3. Fix this by adding a `scale_y_log10()` layer, which puts the y-axis on a log scale.
   And why did we remove genes with a mean count of 0 in step 1?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   gene_means |>
     ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) +
     geom_violin() +
     scale_y_log10()
   ```

   The log of 0 is minus infinity, which can't be plotted:
   _ggplot2_ would remove these genes with a warning.

   </details>

4. Add the individual genes as jittered points on top of the violins.
   Because there are so many genes,
   use the `alpha` and `size` arguments of `geom_jitter()`
   to make the points semi-transparent and small.
   Experiment with their values: which work well?

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>

   `alpha` takes a value between 0 and 1, and the default `size` is 1.5,
   so try values well below these.
   You can also narrow the spread of the points with the `width` argument.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   gene_means |>
     ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) +
     geom_violin() +
     geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5) +
     scale_y_log10()
   ```

   `alpha` ranges from 0 (fully transparent) to 1 (opaque).
   With a low `alpha`, areas with many points look darker,
   so you can still see where most genes are.
   `width = 0.2` reduces how much the points are spread out horizontally.

   </details>

5. Fill the violins by biotype. Does it matter whether you add this mapping
   inside `ggplot()` or inside `geom_violin()`? Try both.

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for a hint_</summary>

   Map `fill` (not `color`) to `biotype` inside an `aes()` call.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   gene_means |>
     ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) +
     geom_violin(aes(fill = biotype)) +
     geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5) +
     scale_y_log10()
   ```

   Here, both give the same plot.
   A global mapping inside `ggplot()` also applies to the points,
   but the default points have no fill (only a color), so they don't change.

   </details>

6. Add a narrow box plot inside each violin with `geom_boxplot(width = 0.1)`,
   without showing the box plot's outliers (you already show all genes as points).
   What does the violin show that the box plot doesn't?
   And which of the two biotypes is more highly expressed?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   gene_means |>
     ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) +
     geom_violin(aes(fill = biotype)) +
     geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5) +
     geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, outlier.shape = NA) +
     scale_y_log10()
   ```

   (With `outlier.shape = NA`, the box plot's outliers aren't plotted twice.)

   A box plot only shows a few summary statistics (the median, quartiles, and outliers),
   while the violin shows the full shape of the distribution.
   For example, the protein-coding genes have a long "tail" of lowly expressed genes.

   Protein-coding genes are much more highly expressed than lncRNA genes:
   note that each step on the log-scale y-axis is a 1,000-fold difference.

   </details>

7. Finish your plot by adding axis labels, removing the legend,
   and applying a theme of your choice.
   Save the plot as an object `violin_plot`,
   and export it to a PNG file in a `results` folder with `ggsave()`.

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} &nbsp; _Click for some hints_</summary>

   - To remove the legend, use `theme(legend.position = "none")`,
     after the theme function like `theme_bw()`.
   - `ggsave()` won't create the `results` folder for you:
     create it first with `dir.create()`, like in the lecture.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   violin_plot <- gene_means |>
     ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) +
     geom_violin(aes(fill = biotype)) +
     geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5) +
     geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, outlier.shape = NA) +
     scale_y_log10() +
     labs(x = "Gene biotype", y = "Mean count across samples") +
     theme_bw() +
     theme(legend.position = "none")

   violin_plot
   ```

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
   ggsave(
     filename = "results/violin_plot.png",
     plot = violin_plot,
     width = 6,
     height = 5,
     dpi = 300
   )
   ```

   </details>

## Exercise 6: Working with Claude

In this exercise, you'll use Claude to polish a plot, and check what it changed.

1. Ask Claude to make your `violin_plot` from Exercise 5 "publication-ready",
   and to add the new version as a separate code chunk below your original one.
   Run the new code chunk.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see an example_</summary>

   Claude's version will differ each time you ask, but here is one example:

   ```{r}
   gene_means |>
     mutate(
       biotype = factor(
         biotype,
         levels = c("protein_coding", "lncRNA"),
         labels = c("Protein-coding", "lncRNA")
       )
     ) |>
     ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) +
     geom_violin(aes(fill = biotype), color = NA, alpha = 0.6) +
     geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.03, size = 0.3) +
     geom_boxplot(width = 0.08, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "white") +
     scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
     scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02")) +
     labs(
       x = NULL,
       y = "Mean read count per gene (log scale)"
     ) +
     theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
     theme(legend.position = "none")
   ```

   </details>

2. Above every line that Claude added or changed,
   add a short comment that explains what the line does, in your own words.
   For anything you don't recognize, check the help page, or ask Claude.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   For the example above, these comments could be:

   ```r
   gene_means |>
     # Set the order of the biotypes, and give them nicer labels for the x-axis
     mutate(
       biotype = factor(
         biotype,
         levels = c("protein_coding", "lncRNA"),
         labels = c("Protein-coding", "lncRNA")
       )
     ) |>
     ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) +
     # Remove the violins' outlines, and make the fill semi-transparent
     geom_violin(aes(fill = biotype), color = NA, alpha = 0.6) +
     # Make the points narrower, more transparent, and smaller
     geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.03, size = 0.3) +
     # Fill the boxes with white, so they stand out from the violins
     geom_boxplot(width = 0.08, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "white") +
     # Show regular numbers like "1,000" on the y-axis instead of "1e+03"
     scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
     # Choose the fill colors manually, using hex color codes
     scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02")) +
     labs(
       x = NULL, # The biotype names speak for themselves
       y = "Mean read count per gene (log scale)"
     ) +
     # A theme without grid lines, with larger text throughout
     theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
     theme(legend.position = "none")
   ```

   </details>
